newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Rival premiers' troops fight in Cambodian capital.
newsitem.headline: Rival premiers' troops fight in Cambodian capital.

text.p: Fighting erupted in Phnom Penh between rival Cambodian government troops on Saturday and the country's "first" prime minister claimed sole legitimate power after accusing his rivals of attempting a coup.
Clashes broke out near the well-fortified compound close to the city centre where top generals and officials loyal to first Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh live.
"We consider that what is currently happening in Phnom Penh is a coup d'etat perpetuated by (second Prime Minister) Mr Hun Sen," said a statement released in Paris in the name of Ranariddh.

In a second statement issued hours later in Paris, where he was said to be visiting family, Ranariddh declared he had become head of Cambodia's only legitimate government as a result of the alleged coup attempt.

"At this time, the sole legitimate government of Cambodia is the one over which I preside, given legitimacy by the free and democratic elections organised by the United Nations in 1993 and by the confidence of the Cambodian people," he said.
The two prime ministers head a deadlocked coalition government set up after United Nations-run elections in 1993.

A long row over power-sharing has been inflamed by deep differences over how to deal with the divided Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, blamed for the deaths of one million people when they ruled in the 1970s and still armed and at large.

Hun Sen, according to Ranariddh, "has attempted a coup d'etat in having his troops intervene on orders of his party, the CPP (Cambodian People's Party), in Phnom Penh...causing the death of numerous innocent civilians".

Ranariddh said the fighting had erupted because Hun Sen "does not want free and democratic elections scheduled for May 1998". He called on the international community not to recognise any regime resulting from the use of force.
Ranariddh also urged Cambodia's armed forces and royal police not to follow Hun Sen and his supporters "in their illegal and criminal adventure, which puts our country in great danger".
Saturday's fighting in the capital of the Southeast Asian country ignited when Hun Sen ordered a crackdown on "illegal troops" under Ranariddh's command.
Witnesses said automatic rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and tanks were used as troops loyal to Hun Sen moved into the compound area and forces loyal to Ranariddh counter-attacked.
Civilians streamed out of the neighbourhood. A Reuters reporter saw one wounded woman.
Intermittent explosions could be heard in the city centre, some five km (3 miles) from the scene of the fighting.
Fighting appeared to subside after nightfall. In a statement broadcast on national television and radio, Phnom Penh municipal authorities said a curfew was being imposed from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
There were also reports of a clash between forces loyal to the rival prime ministers in Battambang province, in northwest Cambodia near the border with Thailand, Cambodian border officials said.
Diplomats in Phnom Penh said there were unconfirmed reports of fighting elsewhere in the country, including southeastern Svay Rieng province.
A pro-Ranariddh general said Hun Sen's forces had captured more than 100 of his men. A radio station run by Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party went off the air without explanation.
Hun Sen's troops blocked main thoroughfares in Phnom Penh and armoured personnel carriers were stationed at strategic locations around the city.
Earlier on Saturday, factional troops battled near a base under Ranariddh's control near Phnom Penh airport. Later in the day there were reports of more clashes near the base.
Major airlines that normally fly into Phom Penh announced cancellations of all flights there on Saturday and said they might do the same on Sunday.

Hun Sen said in a radio and television broadcast earlier on Saturday he had to take action against illegal troops and weapons in order to maintain law and order. He said the fighting did not signal civil war.
Neither of the prime ministers was in the country on Saturday. A Vietnamese official in Hanoi said Hun Sen was on vacation in Vietnam.
Hun Sen has accused Ranariddh's military commanders of bringing defectors from the Khmer Rouge into Phnom Penh to boost his troop strength.

Ranariddh said in his first Paris statement that Hun Sen had seized on his "supposed" negotiations with Khmer Rouge soldiers as a pretext for his actions, which "could sweep away all of the efforts ... to rebuild after 23 years of one of the most pitiless wars of the 20th century".
He said independent investigations had established that there were no hidden Khmer Rouge soldiers to be found in the capital, "including in my own home".
